awd_abstract_narration:
This award provides support for U.S.-based participants of a research conference on dynamics and rigidity, which will take place at the conference center of the Hotel San Michele in Cetraro, Italy. By bringing together experts from various subareas of dynamics, as well as researchers who have applied related methods in groundbreaking ways, the conference aims to foster collaborations across mathematical communities with the ultimate goal of making progress on longstanding problems. An emphasis will be placed on supporting young researchers, with all NSF funds dedicated to providing travel and lodging support for graduate students and postdoctoral scholars. The conference will include professional development panels addressing academic publishing, grant writing, and work-life balance. In addition, organizers will proactively recruiting attendees from a comprehensive range of experts in various stages of their career. Dissemination of knowledge will be ensured through the public availability of resources prepared by the speakers, allowing the broader mathematical community to benefit from the conference's outcomes.

The last several years have seen an unprecedented number of breakthroughs in geometry and dynamics, including the resolution of the Zimmer conjecture, the classification of higher rank orbit closures in strata of Abelian differentials, and the classification of hyperbolic manifolds admitting infinitely many totally geodesic hypersurfaces. Many of these results were direct consequences of new discoveries of rigidity phenomenon in dynamical systems, including the classification of stationary measures following work of Benoist-Quint and applications of Margulis functions as in work of Eskin-Mirzakhani-Mohammadi. The goal of this conference is to bring together experts in rigidity phenomenon and dynamics from several communities, including smooth, homogeneous, and Teichmuller dynamics, together with mathematicians who have successfully applied such results to solve longstanding questions with an eye toward jump-starting collaborations between groups of experts with similar interests and bringing about new and exciting developments. The conference website is https://sites.google.com/view/eskin2025.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
The conference ``Dynamics and Rigidity: A Celebration of the Mathematics of Alex Eskin'' brought together 90 experts in rigidity phenomena and dynamics from various disciplines including smooth, homogeneous, and Teichmüller dynamics. Among them were researchers who have recently applied these ideas in geometry and number theory to solve longstanding problems. More specifically, the conference featured talks by some of the most prominent mathematicians, including a Fields Medalists and four recipients of the Brin Prize in dynamics, offering researchers at all levels exposure to new and transformative ideas. This conference also allowed them to disseminate these powerful techniques to the researchers best poised to use them, including 17 graduate students and 14 postdoctoral researchers. 

A main goal of the conference was to foster the support and professional development of young researchers. Indeed, all funding provided by the NSF was dedicated to sending US-based graduate students and researchers to this conference in order to absorb the powerful new techniques that were being described. Additionally, the organizers organized a professional development panel for early-career mathematicians at the conference.

The last several years have seen an unprecedented number of breakthroughs in geometry and dynamics. These include the resolution of the Zimmer conjecture, the classification of high rank orbit closures in strata of the Hodge bundle, and the recent proof by Avila-Eskin-Viana of the continuity of Lyapunov exponents. Many of these results were direct consequences of new advances in rigidity. This conference brought together experts in rigidity phenomenon and dynamics working in smooth, homogeneous, and Teichmuller dynamics, together with mathematicians who have successfully applied such results to solve longstanding questions. No recent conferences have brought together all of these communities. One year on, some of these collaborations initiated at this conference have developed into breakthroughs in their own right. An example includes work of Apisa and Aygun who classified components of strata of k-differentials in work that began as conversations on the side of this conference. In short, by assembling so many leading lights in the applications of dynamics, the conference stimulated cross-disciplinary collaborations while promulgating new and profound ideas to the current and next generation of researchers in dynamics, geometry, and number theory.
